chapter_theme: The middle of the Ajivika debate: Neelakesi argues that a Lord who knows all and keeps silent is lesser than any speaker, that silence proves nothing and a moving body betrays desire, and that a rainbow is a caused thing; she then attacks Puranan's five atom-kinds (earth alone holding the sensible qualities, darkness outside the five, kinds and substances both one and many), his god's freedom from disease, his denial of merit in giving and of sin in killing, and the identity of quality and substance (the ripening date, the plate made a pot, the classes of words), and opens her attack on the doctrine that every outcome is fixed with the example of an infant girl.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Ajivika teacher at Samadandam who expounds Makkali's doctrine (668)

683.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the Ajivika Lord did not tell all that he knew, then any common man and she herself, who wag their tongues to tell others whatever good they see, are greater than he and stand free of fault in this world and the next.
683.nuance: சாத்தன் in line 2 is the stock name for any man at all; the argument ranks the silent omniscient below the most ordinary speaker. The silence answered is the one Puranan claimed for his Lord in 673 (உரையான் இறைவன்).
683.event: Neelakesi answers the claim that the Ajivika Lord keeps silent and says that ordinary speakers would then surpass him.

claims.claim: an omniscient who does not tell what he knows is lesser than an ordinary man who shares the good he sees
the supreme knower keeps silent and does not teach what he knows

684.reading: Taking up Puranan's comparison of the Lord to the rainbow, Neelakesi says that one with a body and senses is a born being, and that a rainbow is no uncaused marvel but what appears when the sun's rays fall on the rain-cloud: that is its whole nature.
684.nuance: The word சாதகன் in line 2 is read here as 'one who is born'; it could carry another sense, and the division of line 4 (தனுவாம் as 'becomes a bow') is my own.
684.event: Neelakesi turns the rainbow simile for the Ajivika Lord against him.

claims.claim: a being with a body and sense organs is born and caused, like a rainbow that arises from sunlight on rain
the Lord's form is like a rainbow that cannot be grasped

685.reading: Neelakesi asks how Puranan knows that his Lord, who said 'I know all' and then kept silent, really knew; if the proof is that he did not speak, then infants, this tree and the mountain have the same greatness.
685.nuance: Line 2 (னற்ற மகலவென் றானீ) is hard to divide; the sense taken is that the Lord fell silent so that fault would leave him, which matches 682's claim that speaking would bring passion.
685.event: Neelakesi mocks the Ajivika proof of the Lord's omniscience from his silence.

claims.claim: silence is no evidence of knowledge, since infants, trees and mountains are silent too
the Lord's silence after declaring that he knows all shows his perfect knowledge

686.reading: Neelakesi argues that the Lord who bends and stretches his limbs, breathes, walks and sits has not stilled his body, so by Puranan's own reasoning he acts from desire; and if he did none of these, who would grant he had life at all?
686.nuance: The verse turns the Ajivika defence of 682 (that to speak would make the Lord a man of desire and anger) back on him: silence of the tongue leaves the rest of the body in motion.
686.event: Neelakesi argues that the silent Lord's bodily movements betray desire as much as speech would.

claims.claim: if speaking proves passion, every bodily movement proves it too, and a being without movement could not be called alive

687.reading: Neelakesi declares that since the Ajivika has spoken what should not be spoken, the earth-kind, water-kind, fire-kind, the wind-kind and the kind of life, she will not stop harrying him until all who sit near have seen it.
687.nuance: The metre changes here to five-line verses whose last line repeats the fourth with a varied opening; the refrain carries the taunt. The five பால் are the five atom-kinds Puranan set out in 674-677.
687.event: Neelakesi announces before the onlookers that she will confute the Ajivika's five kinds.

claims.claim: the five kinds of earth, water, fire, wind and life are the whole of what exists

688.reading: Neelakesi argues that if colour and the other sensible qualities all belong to the earth-kind, the other three elements, having none, could never be seen by eye or any sense, and so could never be known by any means at all.
688.nuance: The target is 675's claim that every sense-object but sound is earth's; water keeps only its coolness, fire its burning. The objection is that this leaves water, fire and wind unseen.
688.event: Neelakesi attacks the Ajivika assignment of the sensible qualities to earth alone.

claims.claim: all sensible qualities except sound belong to the earth-kind
an element with no sensible quality could be known by no means of knowledge

689.reading: Neelakesi says the Ajivika has multiplied the kinds of water, fire and restless wind by holding only to their names, without examining anything, and so his doctrine, the five he brought forward, collapses.
689.nuance: பிறப்பிறவா in line 2 is not clear to me; it may mean 'without passing beyond birth' or be a corrupt reading.
689.event: Neelakesi declares the Ajivika's doctrine of five kinds overthrown.

claims.claim: kinds distinguished only by name and not by examination give no ground for a doctrine

690.reading: Neelakesi asks, if things are only these five, to which of the five darkness belongs, and if to none, to which the state the Ajivika himself abides in belongs; and are not the compounds made of atoms beyond number?
690.nuance: அருடாழ்ந்து in line 4 may be அருள் தாழ்ந்து, 'sunk in grace' or 'fallen from compassion'; the jibe is unclear. கந்தம் here is the atom-compound of Jain usage, not the Buddhist aggregate.
690.event: Neelakesi challenges the Ajivika to place darkness among his five kinds.

claims.claim: darkness falls under none of the five kinds, so the five do not exhaust what exists
compounds made of atoms are infinite in number

691.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the many kinds he named do not mix and yet are all one substance, he has both oneness and difference at once, and says he has shown no shame at all before the assembly.
691.nuance: சலவாதி may be 'deceitful debater'; சமழலையே is read as 'not ashamed' (சமழ்). Both readings are mine.
691.event: Neelakesi charges the Ajivika with holding both identity and difference of his kinds.

claims.claim: the kinds are many and unmixed yet are the one substance

692.reading: Neelakesi presses: if the one substance becomes the many kinds and there is nothing besides, he must explain how the earth-kind that has turned to ash gives off no smell, and if he is cornered he must establish the same for the other substances.
692.nuance: Line 3's பெறவேலா is unclear; the challenge read is that ash, still earth, has lost earth's smell, so the quality cannot be the substance itself.
692.event: Neelakesi asks the Ajivika why ash, though of the earth-kind, has no smell.

claims.claim: a substance and its kinds are one with nothing besides

693.reading: Neelakesi says that if kinds and substances are not different, listing 'these are kinds, these are substances' as many is like calling one thing hill, mountain, peak and crag: a mere arrangement of words.
693.event: Neelakesi mocks the Ajivika's lists as synonyms for one thing.

claims.claim: if kinds are not different from substances, naming them separately is only synonymy

694.reading: Neelakesi recalls that the Ajivika said the god has no disease, yet one day a sickness hotter than fire came upon him; even dying, she says, Puranan will not come to the truth, so full is his doctrine of wavering and fixed dogma.
694.nuance: The 'sickness hotter than fire' may recall the tradition that Makkali died of a burning fever; the verse names neither the god nor the occasion, and whether கடவுள் here is the founder or the ascetics (கடவுட் குழாம், 668) is not certain.
694.event: Neelakesi cites the burning sickness that struck the Ajivika god against the claim that he is free of disease.

claims.claim: the Ajivika god is free of disease

695.reading: Neelakesi argues that as the hidden planets, though outshone by the sun, still yield their effects at rising and setting, so if all is fixed the beings that have stood through long ages of many births must roam grazing and eating without end, and the Ajivika must accept even fruitless feeding.
695.nuance: The planet simile and the force of உதவாத ஆர்தல் are hard to fix; the reading that the verse attacks the fixed course of births is mine.
695.event: Neelakesi draws an absurd consequence from the Ajivika's fixed course of births.

claims.claim: souls pass through a long fixed course of births that runs its course regardless of their acts

696.reading: Neelakesi asks what this low act of the sinner and fool is: he says that what exists never perishes and what is not never comes to be, yet he says the pure rice he eats in the alms hall has sunk to impurity.
696.nuance: The charge is that calling pure food impure admits a change that the doctrine of 'nothing arises, nothing perishes' forbids; அளி in line 2 is read as the hall where food is given.
696.event: Neelakesi points out the Ajivika's inconsistency over impure food.

claims.claim: nothing that exists perishes and nothing that does not exist comes to be

697.reading: Neelakesi says the Ajivika wants no merit for those who give in every manner, standing, receiving or eating, and holds both that a gift bought by killing is evil and that killing carries no sin; she asks what one who denies the fruit of his own gift has found, and what he has found in austerity above the household life.
697.nuance: Line 3 sets two Ajivika sayings side by side (கொன்றீகை தீது, கொல்பாவம் இல்) as a contradiction. The Neelakesi gives the Ajivika a denial of the fruit of acts; whether the school would accept that account the verse does not show. Line 5 may instead ask what he saw in household life rather than austerity.
697.event: Neelakesi charges the Ajivika with denying the merit of giving and the sin of killing at once.

claims.claim: no merit comes to the giver
killing carries no sin
one who denies the fruit of deeds has no reason to prefer austerity to the household life

698.reading: Neelakesi recalls that when she asked him how ghee turns to flame and burns, if what is not cannot arise and what is cannot perish, he answered only that stones sink and other things float; then, she says, nothing gives room to anything, and he has no cause for sinking and rising.
698.nuance: என்றேனுக்கு in line 2 makes the verse a report of an exchange: her question and his answer. Line 3 (கல்லாந் தயிர்த்தோடி யாழ்மிதப்பு) is hard to divide; the sense of stone sinking and things floating is a guess.
698.event: Neelakesi reports the Ajivika's answer about sinking and floating and rejects it as giving no cause.

claims.claim: atoms never enter one another, and each sinks or rises by its own nature
a doctrine that admits no change gives no cause for sinking and rising

699.reading: Neelakesi says that if the running horse and the horse that eats grass at feeding time are one unchanged thing, let him show her that marvel and she will accept his view and every dogma of his band of 'gods'.
699.nuance: கடவுட் குழாம் is Puranan's own name for the Ajivika ascetics (668), used here in mockery. The point of காநாட்டிய வீதி is not clear.
699.event: Neelakesi challenges the Ajivika to show a thing unchanged through its states.

claims.claim: a thing stays one and unchanged through all its states

700.reading: Neelakesi says that if colour and all the qualities are the substance itself, he should show the greenness seen in the young date-fruit still firm in the ripe fruit; she would call him wise if he could, and a god if he can do it with a thing that has changed.
700.event: Neelakesi tests the identity of quality and substance with the ripening date.

claims.claim: qualities such as colour are the substance itself
a quality changes while its substance remains, so the two are not identical

701.reading: Neelakesi says that since he holds that shape and the like are the substance itself and nothing else, he should show the old shape still present when a plate is broken down and made into a vessel, and show all its changes.
701.event: Neelakesi asks the Ajivika to show the plate's shape in the pot made from it.

claims.claim: shape is the substance itself and nothing other

702.reading: Neelakesi says that when she asks for the things that float and sink, he concludes a plurality of four categories; but if what floats is what sinks and there is nothing else, his words serve nothing, and he has broken his own side at once.
702.nuance: பதப்பொருள் நான்கு in line 2 may be four categories of meaning; what they are is not stated. உதப்பேனும் in line 4 is obscure.
702.event: Neelakesi argues that the Ajivika's own distinctions break his doctrine of identity.

claims.claim: whoever distinguishes floating from sinking things has already given up their identity

703.reading: Neelakesi says that words of action, quality and form are seen distinct when words are separated without error, and joined with their sense they are seen combined by sandhi, but the Ajivika's words fit no rule of grammar.
703.nuance: The argument from grammar is that the three classes of word stay distinct even when joined, as the qualities stay distinct in a thing; the Ajivika's speech is said to break that rule.
703.event: Neelakesi appeals to grammar against the Ajivika's denial of distinct qualities.

claims.claim: language distinguishes action, quality and form words, so the things they name are distinct

704.reading: Neelakesi announces that she will say a few words on the Ajivika claim that what comes to be, the way it comes, the measure to which it comes and the time when it comes are all fixed, and on how that claim falls.
704.nuance: The metre changes again to short four-line verses. The refutation follows in 705 to 707 (the infant girl).
704.event: Neelakesi turns to the Ajivika doctrine that everything is fixed.

claims.claim: what comes to be, how, how much and when are all fixed beforehand

705.reading: Neelakesi sets up her case: take up with proper care the infant girl who is to become a woman, and consider her when she is three cubits tall and when the years stated in their order have passed.
705.nuance: The verse only sets up the example; its point comes in 706 and 707, where the woman's breasts, child and hair would have to be present already in the infant if all is fixed.
705.event: Neelakesi begins an example of a girl child to test the doctrine of fixed outcome.

706.reading: Neelakesi says that, on his view, the nature of the child and the woman she will be, the whole of the seed, already exist without sprouting, and tells him not to hurry, for she will undo his view before it can complete its course.
706.nuance: துறவாளவளும் in line 1 is unclear (perhaps 'she who will not leave it' or 'the renunciant'); the reply is in 707, where breasts, child and hair absent from the infant overturn the view.
706.event: Neelakesi presses the infant example against the fixed-outcome doctrine.

claims.claim: the later states of a being already exist, unsprouted, in its beginning

links.note: Puranan likens his Lord's ungraspable form to the rainbow; Neelakesi makes the rainbow the type of a caused thing, born of sun on rain.
links.teaches: The same rainbow serves the Ajivika as a sign of a form beyond grasping and the Jain as proof that such a form is produced, so the simile decides nothing until its cause is asked.

links.note: 673 praises a Lord who neither ages nor greys; 694 answers with a sickness hotter than fire that came upon the god.
links.teaches: Against a portrait of a Lord without wrinkle or grey hair the Jain debater sets a single bodily event, showing that the debate tests a doctrine by its founder's body as well as by argument.

links.note: The Kural likens the learned who cannot unfold their learning to scentless flowers; Neelakesi ranks a silent omniscient below any man who tells the good he sees.
links.teaches: The couplet faults those unable to expound, and the verse extends the fault to one who could speak and chooses not to, turning a rule about scholars into a test of a god.

gains.a: the verse's mockery gains a recognised Tamil norm that knowledge counts only when it is passed on, which the debate itself never states
gains.b: the couplet, which speaks of inability, gains a case of deliberate silence and a use of its standard in judging a religious founder

links.note: Tirumular says silence of speech alone is mere muteness, true silence being the stilling of mind; Neelakesi says silence of speech proves nothing, since trees and mountains are silent.
links.teaches: Both deny that outward silence shows attainment, but they move the test in opposite directions: Tirumular inward to a stilled mind, the Jain debater outward to the teaching a knower must give.

gains.a: the verse gains a contrast showing that its attack on silence touches only silence of the tongue, not an inner stillness it never discusses
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's distinction gains a debater who uses the same point against a rival's mute Lord, showing that mere muteness was a live charge between schools

links.note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika gives water its own coolness and taste and fire its burning; the Neelakesi's gives every sensible quality but sound to earth alone, and Neelakesi argues the other elements would then be imperceptible.
links.teaches: Set beside the Buddhist report, the Jain objection is seen to strike the version of the doctrine that gives the senses' objects to earth alone; the Manimekalai's Ajivika, who gives water a taste, would be harder to hit.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says the atoms never enter one another, yet move, sink and rise; Neelakesi takes the same premises and demands the cause of sinking and rising.
links.teaches: The two polemics report the same Ajivika premise, atoms that never enter one another and yet sink and rise; the Buddhist leaves it, while the Jain shows it leaves motion without a cause.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says gain, loss, birth and death are mixed in at conception and the fate laid down before brings what follows; Neelakesi tests this with the infant girl whose womanhood must then already be present.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic records the claim that a life's course is fixed at conception and walks away from it; the Jain epic answers it with a concrete reductio, the grown woman's features absent from the infant.

links.note: The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which comes first whatever one devises; Neelakesi attacks a fixity that sets in advance what comes, how, how much and when.
links.teaches: The couplet claims fate outruns human contrivance, but the Jain attack shows that the vulnerable step is the further claim that every particular of an outcome is already fixed, which the couplet does not make.

gains.a: the verse gains a contrast showing that its target is the total fixity of every detail, not every Tamil teaching of fate's strength
gains.b: the couplet gains a measure of how far its claim stops short of the Ajivika determinism that the Jain debater thought refutable

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before an assembly, the loser to yield
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam titles use வாதம்; the id follows earlier Neelakesi chapters

new_concepts.gloss: the fixed: the Ajivika teaching that what comes to be, how, how much and when are all fixed in advance (niyati)
a quality of a thing, lasting or passing, and its relation to the substance that bears it
transformation: a substance passing into new modes, as an unripe fruit ripens or a plate is remade as a pot
new_concepts.label_source: the label is mine, following an earlier Neelakesi chapter; these verses use விகாரம் (701) and திரிந்து (700)

source_issues: 693: lines 4 and 5 had '•' for ஃ (old encoding), repaired by the build.
706: the edition prints the verse number as 7096; it is 706 (the next verse is 707).
693 line 4 ends வேண்டூம் where the refrain in line 5 has வேண்டும்; probably a misprint.
Several lines in 685, 689, 690, 691, 692, 698 and 702 resist word division (e.g. னற்ற மகலவென் றானீ, பிறப்பிறவா, பெறவேலா, கல்லாந் தயிர்த்தோடி); readings there are marked uncertain.
